challengeCorner.prompt: A store had beginning inventory $5,000, purchases $15,000. A physical count showed ending inventory $4,200. Find cost of goods sold.

explanation: A [[kw:periodic inventory system]] relies on a physical count at least once a year; it does not track inventory continuously.
The [[kw:perpetual inventory system]] updates inventory records after every sale and purchase (e.g., scanners at checkout).
Inventory valuation answers two questions: 1) cost of [[kw:ending inventory]] (balance sheet), 2) cost of goods sold (income statement).
The basic formula: $$\text{Cost of Goods Available for Sale} = \text{Ending Inventory} + \text{Cost of Goods Sold}$$
[[imp:Different inventory methods can yield different amounts for ending inventory and COGS, affecting profit.]]

blocks.title: 2. Specific Identification Method

explanation: The [[kw:specific identification method]] assigns the actual cost to each item sold and each item in ending inventory.
It is used when items are unique or high‑value (cars, jewelry, custom goods).

Steps: 1. Sum the cost of all units available for sale. 2. Identify which specific units remain in ending inventory and multiply their quantities by their actual purchase prices. 3. COGS = Goods available – Ending inventory cost.
[[imp:This method matches the physical flow exactly, but it is impractical for large volumes of similar, low‑cost items.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: Blue Company doesn't want to track which specific tubes are left. Instead, it calculates an average cost per tube: $1,200 ÷ 120 = $10.00. Ending inventory = 48 tubes × $10 = $480; COGS = 72 × $10 = $720. This smooths out price fluctuations.

teacherCues: Show the formula: Average cost = Total cost of goods available ÷ Total units available.
Then ending inventory = average cost × units on hand; COGS = average cost × units sold.

visuals.caption: All units—sold and unsold—are valued at the same average cost.
visuals.title: Weighted‑Average for Blue Company

explanation: The [[kw:weighted‑average method]] uses a single average cost for all units.
Step 1: $$\text{Average Cost per Unit} = \frac{\text{Total Cost of Goods Available}}{\text{Total Units Available}}$$.
Step 2: Ending inventory = Average cost × Units on hand.
Step 3: COGS = Average cost × Units sold (or Goods available – Ending inventory).
[[imp:This method is simple and dampens the effect of price changes.]]

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Average Cost} = \frac{\text{Total Cost of Goods Available}}{\text{Total Units Available}}$$ $$\text{Ending Inventory} = \text{Average Cost} \times \text{Units on Hand}$$ $$\text{COGS} = \text{Goods Available} - \text{Ending Inventory}$$
notes: The average cost is not simply the average of purchase prices; it's weighted by the quantities purchased.
Total units available = beginning inventory + purchases.

blocks.title: 4. FIFO (First‑In, First‑Out) Method

discoveryHook.scenario: Blue Company assumes the first tubes purchased are the first ones sold (FIFO). Thus, the 48 tubes left in inventory come from the most recent purchases: 20 from December ($13), 20 from October ($12), and 8 from May ($10). Ending inventory = $260 + $240 + $80 = $580. COGS = $1,200 – $580 = $620. During inflation, FIFO results in higher ending inventory and lower COGS.

visuals.caption: Oldest costs flow to COGS; newest stay in inventory.
visuals.title: FIFO Ending Inventory for Blue Company

explanation: [[kw:FIFO (First‑In, First‑Out)]] assumes the oldest inventory items are sold first.
Ending inventory consists of the most recently purchased units.

Steps: 1. List purchases from earliest to latest. 2. Assign the latest costs to the units in ending inventory, moving backward in time until all ending units are valued. 3. COGS = Goods available – Ending inventory.
[[imp:In periods of rising prices, FIFO produces a higher ending inventory value and lower COGS compared to LIFO.]]

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Ending Inventory} = \sum (\text{Units from Latest Purchases} \times \text{Their Costs})$$ $$\text{COGS} = \text{Goods Available} - \text{Ending Inventory}$$
notes: Work backward from the most recent purchase until the ending inventory quantity is filled.
FIFO approximates physical flow for many products (perishables).
formulaCard.title: FIFO Costing

blocks.title: 5. LIFO (Last‑In, First‑Out) and Comparison

visuals.caption: Different methods lead to different inventory and COGS amounts, affecting profit.
visuals.title: Comparison of Methods for Blue Company

formulaCard.title: LIFO Costing
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Ending Inventory} = \sum (\text{Units from Earliest Costs} \times \text{Their Costs})$$ $$\text{COGS} = \text{Goods Available} - \text{Ending Inventory}$$
notes: Work forward from the earliest purchase until the ending inventory quantity is filled.
LIFO is not permitted under IFRS.

explanation: [[kw:LIFO (Last‑In, First‑Out)]] assumes the newest inventory items are sold first.
Ending inventory consists of the oldest costs.
Steps: 1. Start with the earliest costs and assign them to ending inventory until the required units are reached. 2. COGS = Goods available – Ending inventory.
Comparison: During inflation, LIFO gives lowest ending inventory, highest COGS → lower taxable income. FIFO gives highest ending inventory, lowest COGS. Weighted‑average falls in between.
[[imp:LIFO is allowed in the U.S. but not under international accounting standards.]]
